newsitem.title: INDIA: India introduces bill for non-voting shares.
newsitem.headline: India introduces bill for non-voting shares.

text.p: The Indian government has moved a bill in the upper house of parliament that would amend the Companies Act and enable firms to issue non-voting shares, officials said on Thursday.

A parliament official told Reuters the government wanted to implement the introduction of non-voting shares, as announced in the general budget for 1996/97 (April-March) that was presented in July, through an amendment bill moved on Wednesday.
The government withdrew another bill pending since 1993 for a comprehensive overhaul of company law, saying a fresh look was needed on several aspects, he added.

The bill in the upper house would let companies issue non-voting shares by passing special resolutions at shareholder meetings that specify the price at which the shares are to be issued and provide a higher dividend rate than ordinary shares.
"No company shall be permitted to convert its equity share capital with voting rights into equity share capital without voting rights," the amendment bill says.
It says the non-voting shares shall be entitled to bonus shares and rights shares without voting rights.

Another amendment in the bill would let the government recognise microfilm, computer print-outs and fascimile copies as eligible documents under the law if they are officially authenticated and stored with due care.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said in a statement accompanying the bill that a bill introduced in 1993 to overhaul the Companies Act had not been taken up for consideration because more changes were needed in it.

"In view of suggestions from different forums, the government feels that the bill would require comprehensive revision, keeping in view the changes which have taken place in the capital market, operation of the corporate sector and liberalisation policies," Chidambaram's statement said.

India has changed official rules and eased controls since the launch of an economic reforms programme in 1991. Corporate analysts and officials say the Companies Act needs a thorough overhaul to reflect these controls.
